newsitem.title: ITALY: Italians question promise to reimburse Eurotax.
newsitem.headline: Italians question promise to reimburse Eurotax.

text.p: A government promise to reimburse taxpayers for a stiff "Eurotax" to be imposed in 1997 to enable Italy to join the first wave of countries joining Europe's single currency is taken with a pinch of salt by many analysts.
And the Eurotax, which aims to raise 12.5 trillion lire ($8.3 billion) next year, is not enough on its own to meet the requirements for Europe's economic and monetary union (EMU) .
The credibility of the government's efforts to meet the EMU conditions hang on its ability to introduce essential structural changes in the following year, they said.
In addition, the tax still has to pass the hurdle of approval by the European Commission in Brussels which must decide whether it can count towards the EMU criteria.

Commission officials said on Thursday they would review the tax. They said they were initially unaware that the proposed tax would in effect be returned to taxpayers after a specified period, an arrangement which under normal circumstances would be classified as a loan.
The Eurotax, part of the 1997 budget, will be raised in several ways, including a one-off hike in income tax which the government has promised to reimburse partly, starting in 1999.

"It's just a promise. Nothing will be included in the budget as legislation, it's a political pledge to soothe protest," said Pio de Gregorio, Italian economist at NatWest Markets in Milan of the reimbursement pledge.

Ordinary Italians are wincing at the prospect of yet another tax. Led by the opposition centre-right Freedom Alliance, they have staged huge protests at the austerity plans aimed at squeezing Italy into EMU.
"The government is trying to make the impression this is not a tax but a contribution to be given back once...we have gained a firm chance of acceptance in the EMU club," De Gregorio said.

But EU Commissioner Mario Monti expressed doubt at the pay-back. "The rebate gives the idea more of a loan than an acquired contribution and this, above all abroad, does not give the perception it is a measure aimed at cutting the deficit."

The Bank of Italy forecasts that Italy will struggle to keep this year's deficit below 1995's 130 trillion lire, well over double the 3.0 percent deficit to GDP ratio required in 1997 if a country is to join EMU by the 1999 start date.

The entire 1997 budget package for 62.5 trillion lire of deficit cuts does not bowl economists over because it fails to address structural spending. But they say it is a step which at least sustains the expectation that Italy, even with a delay, could eventually join EMU.

But next year Prime Minister Romano Prodi has to force structural changes mainly in the pension system and welfare spending if he wants to retain the credibility which is helping bring Italian interest rates down and ease interest payments -- the fulcrum of the government's budget balancing act.

"The Eurotax is basically fine...but this was only the first part of the job. Now the government has to look at the second part which is politically more important because it is changing the roots of public spending in Italy," De Gregorio said.
The government hopes to raise 5.5 trillion lire of Eurotax from the income tax hike, while another 3.5 trillion lire is due to come from bringing forward a tax on severance payments.
This could be problematic, warned Riccardo Barbieri, senior economist at Morgan Stanley. "It amounts to borrowing tax payments from the future."

Credito Italiano, in a research note, criticised the measure as having an effect limited to 1997 only, saying there would be a gap in 1998 which must be filled to continue the deficit reduction process.
Barbieri said Italy's tax burden was rising to levels which cause political problems, adding that with a high rate of tax evasion, more hikes had "an asymmetric impact on professions."
Furthermore, while other EU nations were also highly taxed, "what people get in return from the government is very different. I think this is a problem for 1998," he said. ($1=1,499 lire)
